svg.title: A theatre stage recalls that Algernon speaks this line in a comedy.

text.tspan: A theatre stage recalls that Algernon speaks this line in a comedy.
The truth is rarely pure and
never simple.
Algernon Moncrieff (fictional character) · Oscar Wilde · The Importance of Being
Earnest, Act I · Published 1899 · First performed 1895
Algernon has discovered that Jack uses different names in
town and in the country. Pressed to explain himself, Jack
supplies the background to his double identity. Algernon
responds with this polished paradox. In context, the line
belongs to a comedy about social performance and
convenient deception. Its charm need not make Algernon a
reliable moral authority. Readers can admire the wit while
noticing how readily an elegant generalization can excuse
the speaker's own evasions.
Rarely qualifies pure, whereas never makes an absolute
claim about simple. That imbalance gives the sentence its
snap. Its dramatic setting complicates any attempt to treat
it as Wilde's straightforward personal doctrine.
Distinguish an insight about complicated facts from an
excuse for dishonesty in Algernon's remark. (Model: Facts
may resist a simple account, but that complexity does not
make deliberately misleading someone acceptable.)
